title: Your Brain Is Not Showing You Reality
desc: What you see feels like a live window onto the world, but it isn't. Your brain builds it, a fraction of a second late, from scraps, guesses and expectations. In this calm, sourced deep dive we test twelve common beliefs about perception against the science: why your eyes are nothing like a camera, why you never see the present moment, why colour isn't in the objects around you, why people missed a gorilla walking through a game, why a voice can change the sound you hear, why a rubber hand can feel like your own, why pain isn't a simple signal, and why danger doesn't really slow down time. Every claim comes from named studies, with the doubts left in. At the end there is a slow, gentle wind-down, so you can listen until you drift off.
plan: b01: hook (you open your eyes and the room is simply there, sharp, coloured, now) + 'Tonight, we'll explore' list + the method of the night: 12 common beliefs about seeing, each tested against science; open loop: if the brain is guessing, why does it feel so real? (paid off b15)

b02: myth 'your eyes work like a camera': fovea ~2 degrees, sharp vision only in a thumbnail-sized patch at arm's length; saccades about 3 per second; saccadic suppression; the blind spot (Edme Mariotte, 1660s) and how the brain fills it in

b03: myth 'you see the present moment': neural delay (~a tenth of a second); flash-lag effect (Nijhawan 1994, Nature); postdiction (Eagleman & Sejnowski 2000, Science); the stopped-clock illusion / chronostasis (Yarrow et al. 2001, Nature)

b04: myth 'colour is in the object': light vs colour (Newton's prism 1666-1672 'the rays are not coloured'); colour constancy; Adelson's checker-shadow illusion (MIT, 1995); The Dress 2015 (Lafer-Sousa, Hermann & Conway 2015, Current Biology)

b05: myth 'colour words are just labels': Russian goluboy/siniy, Winawer et al. 2007 (PNAS) faster discrimination across the boundary, gone with verbal interference; colour vision differences: colour blindness (~1 in 12 men, ~1 in 200 women), tetrachromacy (Jordan et al. 2010, Journal of Vision)

b06: myth 'you would notice something big': inattentional blindness, Simons & Chabris 1999 (Perception) gorilla ~half missed; Mack & Rock 1998 book; Drew, Vo & Wolfe 2013 (Psychological Science) radiologists 83% missed a gorilla in a lung scan

b07: myth 'you'd notice if things changed': change blindness, Rensink, O'Regan & Clark 1997 flicker; Simons & Levin 1998 door study (person swapped behind a door, about half did not notice); choice of what we store: the world as an outside memory (O'Regan 1992)

b08: myth 'each sense works alone': McGurk & MacDonald 1976 (Nature, 'Hearing lips and seeing voices', ba + ga = da); Shams, Kamitani & Shimojo 2000 (Nature) double-flash illusion; ventriloquism effect

b09: myth 'taste happens on the tongue': the tongue-map myth (Hanig 1901, misread by Boring 1942; receptors for all basic tastes across the tongue, Chandrashekar et al. 2006, Nature); smell makes flavour; Morrot, Brochet & Dubourdieu 2001 (Brain and Language): white wine dyed red described with red-wine words
b10: myth 'you know where your body is': the rubber hand illusion, Botvinick & Cohen 1998 (Nature); Ehrsson 2007 (Science) out-of-body illusion with cameras; proprioception as a constant best guess

b11: myth 'pain is a simple damage signal': Melzack & Wall 1965 (Science) gate control theory; why rubbing a bump helps; phantom limbs and Ramachandran's mirror box (Ramachandran & Rogers-Ramachandran 1996, Proceedings of the Royal Society B)

b12: myth 'seeing is believing, expectations don't matter': Helmholtz's unconscious inference (Handbook of Physiological Optics, 1867); Bruner & Postman 1949 (Journal of Personality) trick playing cards (a red six of spades); the hollow-mask illusion (Richard Gregory); hidden Dalmatian image (a famous photograph by R. C. James)

b13: myth 'time flows at a steady speed / in danger life goes into slow motion': Stetson, Fiesta & Eagleman 2007 (PLoS ONE) 31-metre free fall, own fall judged about 36% longer, but no faster reading of a flickering number; memory, not experience, stretches

b14: myth 'everyone sees the same world': synaesthesia (Simner et al. 2006, Perception, about 4% of people); the brain fills in when input is missing: Charles Bonnet syndrome (Charles Bonnet 1760, his grandfather Charles Lullin); illusions as smart guesses, Muller-Lyer 1889 and Segall, Campbell & Herskovits 1966 (carpentered world)

b15: payoff of the opening loop: perception as prediction (predictive processing; Anil Seth's 'controlled hallucination', book Being You, 2021); why it feels real; what it means for you: humility, kindness when others see it differently, double-checking; recap list of all 12 myths; turn to wind-down

b16: gentle bridge to rest: a window at night: dark adaptation (rods, ~half an hour), Purkinje shift (Purkyne 1825), moon illusion (Kaufman & Rock 1962, Science), old starlight, pareidolia (Liu et al. 2014, Cortex, 'Seeing Jesus in toast')

b17: guided wind-down: eyes closed, the dark is not empty (eigengrau, the grey your brain paints), sounds and touch as the brain's gentle guesses, letting the model rest, callback to the opening room, goodnight, end segment teasing 'How Your Memory Really Works'
